newsitem.title: LATVIA: INTERVIEW-LATVIAN PM SAYS GROWTH, EU KEY TARGETS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-LATVIAN PM SAYS GROWTH, EU KEY TARGETS.

text.p: Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Shkele said on Thursday his main targets for this term are to achieve five percent growth and to start negotiations about membership in the European Union (EU).
"A five percent increase in Gross Domestic Product and successful introduction of negotiations to membership in the EU," Shkele cited as key goals during a Reuters interview.
He said it was very important for Latvia to enter the common market because of the country's history.
"We hope Western democracies will have changed in 50 years so that we won't be sold for the second time," he said.
"But unfortunately one must recognise that someone who has good training in sales, and in doing certain things, is going on doing the same thing once again."
Shkele believes Latvia can achieve the government's long term target of five percent growth in GDP in 1998.
"I hope for 1998, we will be able to reach it and even be over it," he said
Latvian GDP is estimated to have risen over three percent in 1996 and is expected to post a stronger increase this year.
Shkele, an affiliated business man, said he did not think he would run for prime minister in the elections in 1998.
"I doubt it," he said.
Under the rest of this term, Shkele is aiming at balanced budgets. He said this year's general budget will be balanced.
"As for the general budget, I think it will be balanced," he said, adding this included the government and social budget.
He said the local authorities can borrow limited amounts from the state treasury and this could give a smaller deficit in the state's finances.
"That is better than for certain countries in the west," Shkele said.
The budget target is vulnerable to tax revenues falling short of projections.

Shkele said the government had tried to improve its taxation policy but there was still room for improvement and he warned that projections for tax revenue in this current budget may be on the high side.
"There are still some business activities that have not been properly managed from the state. Not all pay taxes," he said.
"Nevertheless, taxation policy has been improving but maybe the figures we have calculated for the near future are too optimistic."

Another crucial goal is good state administration and management. This is one reason why the government has expanded its budget period to stretch over two years with the next budget spanning 1998 and 1999.
"We are looking forward to a two year balanced budget," said Shkele.
He was not worried that the strict budget discipline, keeping government expenditure low, would create social unrest.
"The present policy, that has been strict, is already showing positive results and people are starting to see tangible results," said Shkele.
Yields have fallen from 45 percent in the wake of the banking crisis to around five percent. Inflation fell from 23 percent in 1995 to 13 percent in 1996.
The positive devolopment in inflation is expected to continue this year and the government forecasts nine percent inflation at the year's end.
Shkele was cautious on the future development. Investments will be targeting consumer markets which will influence prices.
"It will not be getting lower than seven percent," he predicted for the end of 1998.
He added that a higher inflation rate would not be harmful if it was caused by large foreign investment. Shkele also said he believed foreign investment in Latvia will take off in 1997.

"I think we will see a breakthrough this year. The biggest enterprises will be privatised, it will activate the capital market and I think the parliament will ratify a very liberal law concerning the land market," he said.
Infrastructure is also being improved, a factor that will help attract investments, he added.
Shkele predicted it would be possible to use land as collateral for long term credits by the end of this year.
